title: The treasure fleets never turned back
premise: In 1433 the Ming court keeps the treasure fleets afloat, and great junks keep linking China to the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. Harbor cities grow rich on silk, porcelain and printed sea charts, and civil examinations welcome navigators and translators from every coast. A thousand harbors come to share one etiquette of trade, study and welcome.

chain.event: The court renews funding for another great voyage and keeps the Nanjing shipyards open.
chain.consequence: Great junks keep sailing the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, and shipwrights train new crews each season.

chain.event: Admirals found permanent lodges with warehouses and chart houses at Malacca, Calicut and Mogadishu.
chain.consequence: Seasonal voyages become year-round harbor quarters where pilots, printers and translators live and teach.

chain.event: The Bureau of Calm Waters begins cheap woodblock printing of sea routes for harbor markets.
chain.consequence: Accurate charts reach fishing towns and island ports, widening navigation far beyond court captains.

chain.event: Civil examinations add navigation, languages and tide reckoning, open to candidates from overseas harbors.
chain.consequence: A shared class of clerks, captains and teachers carries the same etiquette of welcome to every coast.

chain.event: Harbor chart houses link by steam packet and wire signals to share prices for tea, silk and porcelain.
chain.consequence: Inland workshops steady their work for maritime demand and send their children to study at the ports.

chain.event: The Thousand Harbors Concord agrees on common signals, pilot guidance and school standards.
chain.consequence: By 2026 the oceans work as one peaceful market of exchange halls, study pavilions and festivals.
